extracted.intended_audience: general readers; journalists, students, and researchers interested in photojournalism and media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards about ethical, editorial, and legal expectations for news photographers and news organizations, illustrated by the Brian Walski doctored-photo incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on altering news photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Brian Walski... was accused in 2003 of altering a news photograph, which he later admitted to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altering news photographs is treated as a serious ethical violation by news organizations (example: Walski was accused and admitted alteration). The page presents alteration as a behavior that breaches professional norms and leads to disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: No compositing of separate frames to improve composition
rubrics_metrics.description: He decided to use his computer to combine two of the images that had been taken a few seconds apart into a single image with better overall composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining two separate photos taken seconds apart to produce a more dramatic/‘better’ composition is presented as a deceptive manipulation that misrepresents the scene; the incident is used to illustrate that such compositing is unacceptable in news photography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial verification and detection of inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: It was at the Courant, on whose front page the image was published six columns wide, that inconsistencies in the image were noticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms and editors must examine images for inconsistencies; other publications or copy editors may detect manipulation. The example shows publication-wide review and cross-checks can reveal faked images before or after wide distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational responsibility to retract and explain errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Los Angeles Times ran an immediate retraction, and on April 2 it ran a front-page article explaining Walski's faked image, illustrated by the two source images and the manipulated image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When manipulation is discovered, the appropriate response shown is prompt retraction and transparent explanation, including publishing the original source images alongside the manipulated image to document the error and correct the public record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for manipulation — employment and reputational sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: As a result of manipulating the photograph, Walski was fired from the Los Angeles Times via satellite phone on April 1, 2003.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Image manipulation can result in immediate termination and significant reputational harm; the page uses Walski's firing as an example of typical institutional consequences for breaching photojournalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural handling and distribution responsibilities for staff photographers
rubrics_metrics.description: He then sent the pictures to Los Angeles Times staff who posted them on the internal photo sharing system for various media outlets owned by the Tribune News Corporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographers and staff who distribute images (e.g., via internal sharing systems) bear responsibility for the authenticity of those images; news organizations must have procedures governing submission, posting, and vetting of staff images before broader distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining public trust as a core ethical imperative
rubrics_metrics.description: Altered Photos Break Public's Trust in Media (referenced commentary on the incident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The incident is cited in discussions of trust and deception in media: preserving authenticity and avoiding manipulative practices are necessary to maintain public trust in journalism; manipulated images undermine credibility and provoke industry-wide responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of ethical and legal considerations in photojournalism
rubrics_metrics.description: See also: Ethical and legal considerations in photojournalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page points readers to broader ethical and legal frameworks (e.g., NPPA guidance, media ethics texts) that govern acceptable practices, implying that photographers should follow established codes and legal norms regarding image integrity.
